title: Messier 72 shines again
caption: The globular cluster Messier 72, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 72, NGC 6981 · constellation Aquarius · about 50,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, A. Sarajedini, G. Piotto, M. Libralato

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week, April 2025 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A round, tightly packed cluster of stars glitters in this new Hubble view of Messier 72, a globular cluster about 50,000 light-years away in Aquarius. The strong gravity binding its stars gives it a regular, round shape.

M72 holds a special place in Hubble history: it was the very first ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week, released on 22 April 2010. Fifteen years and close to 800 pictures later, the team returned to it with new data and processing.

The new colors come from adding ultraviolet observations to the earlier visible-light ones, and they pick out different groups of stars. Blue stars began more massive and now burn hotter after using up much of their hydrogen. The bright red ones are lower-mass stars that have swollen into red giants. Telling these groups apart helps show how globular clusters, and their galaxies, came together.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (3.24 × 3.27 arcminutes) and its distance of about 50,000 light-years, the frame spans roughly 47 × 48 light-years. Its light set out about 50,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble’s cameras through five filters, from ultraviolet (275 nm) to near-infrared (814 nm). The color assigned to each filter isn’t published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the colors are assigned, so the eye would not see this palette.

explore: Pierre Méchain, a French astronomer who worked with Charles Messier, discovered M72 in 1780, the first of five clusters he found while helping Messier. It is one of the most distant clusters in Messier’s catalog. The 2010 version is also in this collection.
alt: A dense, round cluster of white, blue and red stars on a dark background.
